title: Gangsters at the Cotton Club and a show at Sing Sing
summary: Gangsters were friendly, well-dressed bosses who ran the Cotton Club; Cab's whole show once played Sing Sing for an imprisoned mobster.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: I mean the gangsters, did they look like those people we see in the movies?
Yeah, they were very fine dressers,

but nice, friendly, but you could tell they were the boss, you know, a lot of them came in the Cotton Club, when I was with Cab, I knew a lot of them, they came over. We went to Sing Sing and played a little benefit, a whole Cotton Club show for one of the mobsters up there, he was in there.
That was during the time I was with Cab, at the Cotton Club.
You went to Sing Sing to play specifically for this one mobster?
Well, you see, I'm going to tell you something, you know, the Cotton Club was I think the -- as far as I know, most all of the Cotton Club was run by the mobsters, I think, that's what I heard.
They had to have some connection at Sing Sing in order to arrange that.

Yes, cause I remember I used to drink a little beer at the time, beer we used to drink up there, I forget the name of that beer, but they said it was all mobster controlled. The beer -- all the beer at the Cotton Club, and I'm quite sure they had a lot to do with the Cotton Club.
I'm quite sure they did. Because that
was money, I knew they would come in, they would come in there on weekends and they would take over.
You remember what year that was you played at Sing Sing?

Well that was during Cab's heyday, it was in the '30's. I don't exactly remember the year. It was either '30, before we did the "Big Broadcast." Cause we would go right from the Cotton Club in a bus, meet there and go right straight to Sing Sing and did this whole show, and all the girls the whole entire show, we played Sing Sing, for one of the fellows was up there serving time.
